holding one of those huge cheeses to the fire and scraping off what

From the window of this truly top-side spot
we could see the Matterhorn, Weisehorn and many other famous
mountsins.
We returned to Geneva that same Sunday night.
The next
two days, i.e. Monday and Tuesday, were devoted to sessions of IATA,
Lunches,
cocktail parties and dinners of the usual variety, Wednesday
we had a free day and all went on a special train to the Lausanne
Fair which was much like any county fair at home - lunch overlooking
the Lake and afterwards a boat trip to the famous castle of Chillon
Dat trity tort at home -0
neer the upper end of the Lake. Our boat landed at a dock near this
castle made famous by one of Lord Byron's best known poems,
"Prisoner
of Chillon".
It was dark as we all walked along the path, but as
we approached the drawbridge men dressed in medieval costumes lined
the path and each held aloft a flaming torch. As we got closer
trumpets were sounded from the ramparts of the dirk castle wall.
It was thrilling end put on in the best Hollywood tradition, sans
corn.
You could easily imagine yourself transported back to the
15th Century when the Duke of Savoy ruled that part of the world
and Bonnivard was his prisoner.
We entered - all of IATA this time,
some 300 men and women - the castle and there in a huge stone vaulted
hell lighted only by candles we had as delicious a dinner as you
have ever had with, of course, four different kinds of wine.
Then
a group of Swiss men and girls in native costume sang for us. The
songs were all local ballads except for the rendition in French with
considerable vuriation of "My Old Kentucky Home". (Sam and Frances
please note.) We learned afterwards that few parties are allowed
in the castle and that this was the largest one on record.
The rest of the week was a continuation of the more
routine affairs,
ending in a big dinner Thursday night.
The General
Meeting adjouned Friday noon and our Executive Meeting
late that
afternoon.
Later - Debby and I are now at the Hotel du Lac at
Interlaken.
We left Geneva at 11:00 AM this morning by train and
went around the Loke to Montreux.
There we chenged to a small,
narrow gage railroad which climbed up over the mountains into
the
high country just below the snow line.
Weather was bright sunshine
and
the visibility good. Scenery magnificent. Little villages
snuggling in quaint valleys with cattle grazing on the green hillsides.
up to where the snow fenced them in.
It was a wonderful experience
and gave us an insight on the way the Swiss live in the relatively
little-traveled hinterland.
ve had checked our baggage through to
Interlaken and didn't mind the four changes of trains in the five
nour trip.
Tomorrow, Sunday the 2lst, if the wether is good we're
going up the Jungfrau by train.

Later - Mondsy Morning, September 22nd.
You remember the irishman who described the weather by
saying, "If you con see yonder hill it is going to rain.
If you
can't see it, it's raining."
That's what
we feared
when we went
to bed Saturday night. You can imagine our joy Sunday morning
when we arose early to see the sun shinging brightly and not s
cloud in the sky. Our train ran along the Lake for & little way
and then headed up a valley where we soon changed to another with
gears which followed a steel gear-way between the tracks.
Then we
started up - and I mean up. After a couple of hours we changed agein
to a smaller lighter car and now above the timberline we moved more
slowly as well as steeply with the most/remendous scenery all around
us.
Presently we entered a tunnel carved out of the solid rock
and for 45 minutes we stayed in that tunnel moving always ever higher
until we arrived at a spot some il,000 feet high. There against a
clear blue Arizona sky was the Jungfrau peak surrounded by other
mountoins interspersed with glaciers, and everywhere deep, deep
snow.
It was o sight from a site which we shall never forget and
weren't we lucky to have such a perfect dey! This morning as I write
in our hotel room it is raining hard and the visibility is perhaps
a quarter of a mile with a 3 to 400 foot ceiling.
We're leaving
at 10:30 for Lucerne and I'll carry on from there.
Later - Lucerne
Lovely trip over the mounteirs and along the shores of
small lakes. Switzerland looks like a well-keit golf course without
bunkers or rough.
sinile.
There is seemingly
no problem of rags and riches.
There must be lots of rich people
but they have the good taste not to swagger.
There must be lots
of poor people but we haven't seen any evidence of poverty.
Lake Lucerne is beautiful - something like Lake George
except thet the mountains are rough and rugged - more like a 10,000'
Shelving Rock with snow perpetuslly on the top. I'll still take
Topside and Lake George.
Later - Monday Evening, late
We loved Lucerne.
It is quaint and different.
he arrived
in time for lunch then drove around the city and out into the
country.
Then we walked around the old section with its narrow
streets, little squares and walls with pictures painted on them.
We saw the Lion of Lucerne.
After dinner Charlie Sendmeyer, PAA
District Sales Manager at Zurich who commutes there from here,
came by to see us.
He asked us to have a drink at the Old Swiss
House, and of course we readily egreed.
Mr. Buholzer - Gussie
Busch's f ther-in-law, showed us around the family living quarters
above the restaurant.
Shades of Dr. Sayman! Or the Buschs- take
your choice.
We entered through an old convent l6th century gate
and from then on it was one museum
piece after another.
One, a
huge tile stove with a circular set of steps leading to a single
chair - also
tile - where one could sit warmly if not hot. In their

bedroom were pictures of Gussie at Grants Farm driving a four-in-hand
with that dope Harry Truman as co-pilot.
A large picture of Gussie
and his bride.
According to our man Sandmeyer she is a very nice
girl and certainly her family are
sound, substantial people.
Enroute Zurich-Paris in a Swissair DC-3 - September 23rd
there. I hope to be in New York by October 7th, spend a few days
1 to 50. 5o in Her fork be
We're due in Paris at 11:00 AM and I'll mail this from
Paris where I'll pick up the better half of the family and we'll go
to Tokyo.
All the best to all of you from us both.
Harold
